title: Where a child lives can shape later opportunity because housing markets do not price or finance all opportunity well
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35419, U.S.-centered review of experimental and quasi-experimental neighborhood-effects evidence and opportunity-market failures
geography: United States; childhood neighborhoods, residential sorting, housing mobility, and mixed-income policy

observations.period: Review of experimental and quasi-experimental evidence on childhood neighborhoods and long-term socioeconomic outcomes

denominator.unit: Multiple studies and policy settings summarized in a review; no single pooled-person denominator

neighborhood_effects.value: the reviewed evidence finds substantial causal impacts of childhood neighborhoods on adult earnings and other long-term socioeconomic outcomes

market_failures.value: capital-market limits on borrowing against children's future earnings, neighbor spillovers, behavioral biases, and housing-search frictions can support excessive income-based segregation and under-supply of mixed-income neighborhoods

policy_routes.value: customized housing-mobility services combined with subsidized vouchers can help low-income families move to higher-opportunity areas; place-based mixed-income policies appear to improve long-term outcomes for less-advantaged children

household_conversion.value: not observed as one common outcome in the review
household_conversion.unit: missing same-family search effort, lease-up, school experience, safety, cost, continuity, and adult outcome ledger

observations.method: Review and synthesis of experimental and quasi-experimental studies on neighborhood exposure, residential sorting, housing mobility, and place-based policy; the paper is not a single new pooled experiment.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not provide a common denominator, one effect size, or a single policy implementation estimate. The mechanisms and policy conclusions combine findings from different studies, places, cohorts, and interventions that should not be treated as one pooled result.
observations.subgroup: Children and families differentiated by parental income and residential opportunity; the abstract does not provide a complete common breakdown by race, disability, family structure, transportation, or local housing market.
observations.counterinterpretation: Neighborhood selection, school access, family resources, and policy implementation can differ across studies. A move to a higher-opportunity area may impose search, transport, care, social-network, rent, or safety costs, and a place-based intervention may improve some long-term outcomes without producing immediate household stability.

related_sources.claim: HUD voucher administrative evidence supplies a separate lease-up and search-time conversion boundary.

boundary: This review record summarizes U.S.-centered evidence that neighborhood exposure and housing-market failures can shape long-term opportunity. It does not provide one pooled causal estimate, show that every voucher or mobility service improves outcomes, or follow one family from housing search through durable adult security.
